LONDON, Oct 19 : Uber on Monday said it had won its bid to throw out two linked lawsuits valued at around £340 million ($453 million) brought by thousands of London black cab drivers and two former private hire companies. The ride-hailing app was sued in 2024 over allegations about how it obtained a private hire vehicle operating licence in the British capital, with the claimants alleging Uber gave "misleading and inaccurate information" to Transport for London. Uber denied the allegations and also argued the lawsuits were filed after the six-year limitation period for bringing such a claim, meaning they should be thrown out. A copy of the High Court's ruling was not immediately available.

Source: Reuters

TOKYO, Oct 19 : Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said on Monday she would not rule out the chance of issuing bonds to fund a two-year cut to the country's consumption tax scheduled from April next year. The government will seek to stably lower the ratio of debt balance to gross domestic product (GDP) by reviewing both spending and expenditure, Takaichi told parliament. "As we do this, we will appropriately control the size of annual bond issuance," she said. "We would not rule out the chance of issuing bonds altogether," Takaichi said, highlighting how the government could raise proceeds to fund the scheduled sales tax cut. Takaichi also said Japan can heighten market trust in the yen by pursuing steps to strengthen the economy. The government has laid out a plan to cut an 8 per cent levy on food items from April next year, as part of efforts to cushion the blow to households from rising living costs.

Source: Reuters

SOPOT, Oct 19 : Polish satellite maker Creotech Instruments plans to raise its production capacity by up to tenfold by 2029, CEO Grzegorz Brona said on Friday, while warning Europe would remain reliant on US rockets to put its satellites into orbit for years. Brona spoke with Reuters in Sopot two days after Ukraine said SpaceX had curbed its use of Starshield, the military-grade version of the Starlink satellite network. Shares of Eutelsat, widely seen as Europe's leading challenger to Starlink, jumped 23 per cent on Wednesday and closed the week 28 per cent higher. Asked whether European industry could build an alternative to Starlink, Brona said the continent could produce thousands of satellites and still have no one to launch them. "Launch vehicles are now becoming a means of political pressure on the European Union in the hands of (US President) Donald Trump's administration," he said.

Europe carried out 8 of the world's 324 orbital launches last year, against 193 by the US. Starlink alone accounted for more than 60 per cent of active satellites, according to European Space Agency data. Creotech, which does not build rockets, has kept US technology out of its satellites to avoid US arms export rules, under which Washington can block sales of a satellite containing even a small American part. Yet it still relies on US rockets. SpaceX carried all four satellites Creotech built for Poland's MikroGlob military programme into orbit. "Of course, Europe is waking up," Brona said, pointing to new European rocket programmes including a German launcher, but added that building enough rockets would probably take a decade. Separately, he said programmes for several large EU satellite constellations — fleets of spacecraft working as one system — were already under way, and that Creotech aimed to bid in their tenders. The satellite maker plans to open a factory in 2029 able to make 40 satellites a year of mixed types, or up to 100 of one model, compared with about 10 at its current plant. Brona added Creotech would start opening subsidiaries in France and Germany in the coming weeks and was aiming to build 500-kg satellites by 2032. Revenue for next year is secured, and the company will probably sign several more contracts within six months, Brona said.

(Writing by Rafal Nowak and Emmanuelle Serres in Gdansk;Additional reporting by Alicja Surdy; Editing by Milla Nissi-Prussak)

Source: Reuters

SEOUL, Oct 19 : South Korea's financial regulator said on Monday that SK Hynix's potential listing of US unit Solidigm could violate restrictions on dual listing.  Financial Supervisory Service Governor Lee Chan-jin said at a parliamentary hearing that South Korean regulators were looking into whether Solidigm's potential initial public offering in the United States would require a review under domestic rules.  "We keep monitoring the issue ... both the Financial Services Commission and ourselves judged that it is a violation of [rules on] dual listing," Lee told a lawmaker when asked how regulators would protect the interests of minority shareholders in parent SK Hynix if Solidigm went public. "The FSC has been waiting for an official interpretation of the rules on whether the issue is subject to filing for domestic securities registration," he added, referring to the top financial regulator.

FAST

SINGAPORE: Indonesian stocks slid to a six-year low on Monday (Oct 19) as a warning from MSCI over possible expulsion from its global indexes next year rattled fragile investor sentiment, sharpening the focus on how Jakarta intends to allay the index provider's concerns. Jakarta's benchmark stocks fell over 5 per cent in early trading on Monday after plunging 11.6 per cent on Friday , as the world's worst performers reeled from index provider MSCI saying it was considering shifting Indonesia to "standalone" status from its current "emerging markets" mantle. A shift to standalone status would risk cutting Southeast Asia's biggest economy off from international capital, relegate it to an investment backwater and club it with a group of standalone markets that includes Lebanon and Zimbabwe. The more-severe-than-expected move has raised the stakes for Indonesia's regulators and finance officials.

On Monday, the Indonesia Stock Exchange said it cut its lower auto-rejection limit to 7 per cent from 15 per cent to give investors "an opportunity to evaluate and digest available information, helping them make better investment decisions based on Indonesia's economic fundamentals". The move followed a weekend meeting between the financial regulator and capital market participants, including analysts and economists. An Indonesian regulator on Friday also unveiled sanctions against those linked to alleged trading manipulation in shares of three firms, with the fines totalling 2.1 trillion rupiah (US$116.4 million). Angus Mackintosh, an ASEAN specialist at Aletheia Capital in Singapore, said the fact the fines were announced on Friday suggests that Indonesia's Financial Services Authority (OJK) has been working on the matter for a while. "The fines are a positive move, but there needs to be concerted action to stamp the authority of the OJK and take direct action against certain well-known players who have been involved in market abuse," he said. MSCI had threatened a downgrade to "frontier" status in January because of opacity in ownership and trading behaviour but said on Friday the lack of progress in remedying those concerns meant even a drop to that status would not reflect the severity of the issues.  "The burden of proof has shifted: avoiding reclassification will require clear evidence that the announced reforms have been consistently implemented and materially improved market functioning," strategists at Goldman Sachs said in a note.

Related:

Indonesia clings to emerging markets mantle as MSCI extends review to November

Rupiah slide and ‘Sell Indonesia’ stocks: Jakarta’s counter moves useful but experts flag deeper fiscal concerns

WIDER RISKS FROM MSCI'S WARNING Goldman Sachs estimates a full MSCI removal could trigger US$5.6 billion of passive outflows. Active funds benchmarked to these indexes hold more than US$8 billion, although any selling would be discretionary rather than benchmark-driven, they wrote. Foreign investors have net sold US$4.88 billion worth of Indonesian stocks so far this year, on track for the biggest annual outflow in at least 16 years.  Aninda Mitra, head of Asia macro and investment strategy at BNY Investments, said foreign equity exposure to Indonesia has shrunk to the point where "there may not be much more downside from here." "But at the same time, even if there are some interesting and fundamentally sound companies and banks, attracting sufficiently large amounts of capital will be tougher in this environment," he said.   MSCI's warning raises the stakes for the government of President Prabowo Subianto, which has faced a series of setbacks this year, with Moody's and Fitch having cut their sovereign rating outlooks to negative earlier in 2026.   Investors are also fretting over the ramifications beyond the US$500 billion stock market, with the rupiah weakening to 18,040 per dollar, not far from the record low of 18,190 hit in June.  "Our bigger concern is not index-related selling itself," said Gary Tan, portfolio manager at Allspring Global Investments in Singapore, "but the potential near-term spillover into the rupiah and domestic bond yields, where market dislocation could translate into tighter financial conditions and a more meaningful impact on the real economy."

Source: Reuters/ec

SYDNEY: Asian share markets mostly slipped on Monday (Oct 19) as unease over AI's enormous funding needs undermined confidence ahead of a week packed with earnings, while Chinese economic data pipped forecasts in a positive for world growth. A fall in oil prices offered some support to bonds and Wall Street stock futures, limiting Asia's losses. Oil fell following US President Donald Trump's decision to waive some sanctions on Russia, though he later said a final decision on the matter had not been made. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Saturday that the president would take up to 60 days to assess the economic impact of such a move. Brent futures still fell 1.8 per cent to US$107.83 a barrel, while US crude futures lost 1.2 per cent to US$100.20 a barrel. Meanwhile, Iran reported another tanker had hit a mine in the Strait of Hormuz, while the cost of shipping and insurance was keeping oil prices for actual delivery a lot higher.

Geopolitical tensions combined with safe-haven flows from equities to extend a rally in sovereign bonds, with 10-year Treasury yields down 4 basis points at 5.0525 per cent, having just recorded their largest weekly fall in over eight months. All of this helped S&P 500 futures edge up 0.8 per cent, while Nasdaq futures rose 1.3 per cent. Asian markets were hampered by concerns about tech and Japan's Nikkei fell 0.7 per cent, after losing 5.4 per cent last week. South Korea added 0.6 per cent, having shed more than 14 per cent last week, while Taiwan fell 1.1 per cent. MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan eased 0.2 per cent. "Investors have long worried that AI revenues won't be sufficient to recoup the massive upfront investment, while AI infrastructure may need to be written down as it ages and depreciates in the meantime, which lowers book value massively," said My Bui, an economist at fund manager AMP. "Rising government bond yields and wider corporate credit spreads are increasing financing costs, making it harder to borrow, refinance, and keep the AI infrastructure build-out going." Jakarta's equity benchmark slumped 5 per cent as the world's worst performer reeled from index provider MSCI saying it was considering shifting Indonesia to "standalone" status from its current "emerging markets" mantle. Chinese blue chips nudged up 0.1 per cent after data showed the economy grew 4.5 per cent in the third quarter to just pip forecasts. Retail sales were also better with a rise of 1.1 per cent, while industrial output growth came in on forecasts at 5.5 per cent. China's yuan also firmed to its strongest level since July 2022 at 6.6828.

Related:

China's economy picks up pace in Q3 as exports power uneven recovery

Indonesian stocks slide to six-year low as MSCI warning weighs

A LOT RIDING ON EARNINGS The PHLX Semiconductor Index shed 11.4 per cent last week in its longest losing streak since 2008. Investors will be hoping Meta will beat Wall Street forecasts when it announces earnings on Wednesday, when semiconductor firms Lam Research and Texas Instruments and Elon Musk-led Tesla also report. Results from Musk's SpaceX are due Tuesday. Meta is one of five AI hyperscalers that combined are expected to increase their capital spending to about US$1.2 trillion next year, according to Goldman Sachs. Meta alone expects to spend US$130 billion to US$145 billion on capex in 2026, and any increase in that could unsettle investors. The group needs to make US$62.5 billion to just hit the midpoint of its own revenue guide. Others reporting this week include Netflix, Procter & Gamble, General Motors and GE Aerospace. Earnings are still expected to rise 30 per cent overall thanks to the huge profits made by tech firms. European stocks were weighed down by political uncertainty in France with EUROSTOXX 50 futures off 0.3 per cent, while DAX futures lost 0.2 per cent and FTSE futures eased 0.1 per cent. Those same concerns saw the euro dip 0.1 per cent to US$1.1232, nearer to last week's 16-month low of US$1.1113. The dollar was flat on the yen at 158.07 and has spent the entire month so far in a tight range as the threat of Japanese intervention has kept speculators at bay. In commodity markets, non-interest-bearing gold got a lift from falling yields and rose 0.4 per cent to US$4,181 an ounce.

Source: Reuters/ec

TOKYO: Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda said underlying inflation is "quite close" to the central bank's 2 per cent target with strong global AI demand adding to inflationary pressure from a tight job market, signalling scope for further rate increases. The remarks came ahead of the central bank's key policy meeting later this month, where it will release fresh quarterly growth and inflation forecasts which will be scrutinised by markets for clues on the next interest rate-hike timing. "It is becoming more important to anchor underlying inflation around our 2 per cent target," Ueda told parliament on Monday. While rising raw material costs from the Middle East conflict were pushing up inflation, a tight job market and moderate economic recovery were also applying demand-driven price pressure, Ueda said.

"Very strong global AI demand is boosting capital expenditure and exports, thereby pushing up prices for a wide range of goods," he said. Ueda also said raising interest rates at an appropriate pace would help avoid spikes in bond yields. "As underlying inflation approaches 2 per cent and financial conditions remain accommodative, failing to adjust our policy rate appropriately could push up long-term interest rates by stoking market concern over an inflation overshoot," he said. The BOJ has a two-day policy meeting that concludes on October 30. Having just raised rates in September, many in the BOJ are cautious about delivering another hike this month and prefer to gauge more data on how past rate increases have affected financial conditions, sources have told Reuters. Many market players expect the BOJ to keep interest rates steady at 1.25 per cent but drop hints that leave open scope for a hike to 1.5 per cent as early as December. CONTROLLING DEBT ISSUANCE Japanese government bond (JGB) yields have risen on prospects of further BOJ rate hikes and concerns that Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's big spending plans could worsen the country's already strained finances. When asked by an opposition lawmaker about the impact of fiscal spending on inflation, Ueda said increased expenditure would push up price and wage growth by stimulating the economy. But if increased fiscal spending boosts Japan's supply capacity, that in turn could help moderate inflation in the long run, he added. Ueda reiterated that emergency bond-buying would be reserved for episodes of sharp yield rises or serious market dysfunction. Speaking in the same parliament session, Takaichi dismissed suggestions by some analysts that her administration's policies had triggered the selloff in the yen and JGBs. "We will meticulously scrutinise the size of fiscal spending and appropriately control the size of debt issuance," Takaichi said. "By creating a strong economy, Japan can heighten market trust in the yen," she added. The JGB market has steadied after the administration sought to dispel perceptions of a reflationist agenda. But analysts expect renewed turbulence if the government fails to clarify how it would fund its tax-cut and big spending plans. The International Monetary Fund last week urged the BOJ to keep raising interest rates, and for the government to lay out a medium-term fiscal framework to soothe market jitters. "Markets are concerned about the fiscal risks because of the uncertainty" on how Japan would pay for the fresh spending and tax-cut plans, Krishna Srinivasan, director of the IMF's Asia and Pacific Department, told Reuters.

Oct 19 : A unit of Japan's Daiichi Life has made an indicative proposal to buy more than 79 per cent of shares in Australian investment manager Challenger it does not already own, Challenger said on Monday. Shares of the Australian firm jumped over 15 per cent to A$11.33 by 2305 GMT, hitting their highest level since October 23, 2018. Under the proposal, the Japanese insurer is offering A$11.80 apiece, valuing Challenger at A$7.94 billion ($5.53 billion). The offer represents a premium of 19.8 per cent over the stock's closing price on Friday. The unit, TAL Daiichi Life Australia Pty, holds 20.36 per cent of the Australian investment manager, according to LSEG. Daiichi Life, through its unit, had initially acquired a 15.1 per cent minority stake in Challenger from MS&AD Insurance Group Holdings in April 2025.

Oct 18 : AI lab Anthropic, the developer of Claude, said on Sunday it will commit 5 per cent of its shares to a new public benefit fund so it has increased flexibility and scale to make donations for the "public good." The proposed fund would be established as a wholly owned limited liability company and would receive an additional 2 per cent of Anthropic's shares, at the board's discretion, for every 50 per cent increase in the company's value above a baseline that has yet to be disclosed. The move comes at a time when Anthropic is planning one of the biggest IPOs in history as a public benefit corporation, a legal structure that requires management to consider certain broader interests as well as turning a profit for investors. The company, which has positioned itself as a safety-first AI lab, has said AI could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity" and devoted roughly 80 pages of the 261-page main body of its prospectus to laying out risk factors.

Anthropic said in its blog post its Public Benefit Fund could support initiatives including nonprofit donations, direct distributions to specific populations and efforts to address AI’s impact on the labor market.  Elon Musk, who runs Anthropic rival xAI, on X said he recommended "giving the shares directly to the public." Anthropic cited the potential impact of AI on workers as one area of focus for the new fund, building on a previously announced $200 million commitment to study and address labor-market disruption. Global companies have cut thousands of jobs after investing heavily in AI, with many, primarily tech firms, pointing to higher efficiencies from the technology's rapid adoption. IMF research shows that some 40 per cent of jobs will be either augmented, downgraded or eliminated by AI, with the number as high as 60 per cent in advanced economies, Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said last week. NOT FOR POLITICAL GIVING The AI giant said none of the equity held by its fund would be used for lobbying or political giving in the United States or abroad. US policymakers are weighing greater oversight of artificial intelligence and AI companies are stepping up efforts to shape how the technology is regulated. Combined with its co-founders' pledge to donate 80 per cent of their equity and an employee donation matching program, roughly 20 per cent of Anthropic's shares will be dedicated to public purposes, excluding any additional shares added later. Anthropic said it would say more in the coming months on the fund's governance, structure and the valuation thresholds that could expand its ownership stake. It also plans to publish a public-benefit report detailing progress toward its mission.

Source: Reuters

SEOUL, Oct 18 : Samsung Electronics will use TSMC's 3-nanometre process to produce base dies for Nvidia's next-generation custom high-bandwidth memory (HBM) chips, the Seoul Economic Daily reported on Sunday. The move would mark the first time Samsung has worked with the Taiwanese contract chipmaker at the HBM manufacturing stage, according to the report. • Nvidia has asked Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron Technology to use TSMC's process for NVHBM base dies, and sixth-generation DRAM technology for its core dies, the newspaper said, citing industry sources. • NVHBM, unveiled in August, integrates Nvidia's custom memory controller into the base die and is aimed at standardising implementation across multiple memory suppliers, according to the company.

Oct 18 : Microsoft has pulled out of a data center deal with British cloud provider Nscale, Britain's Telegraph newspaper reported on Sunday. The US tech giant, one of Nscale's two largest customers, recently terminated its agreement for the data center in Loughton, Essex, according to the report. The newspaper did not specify why Microsoft withdrew from the project. Microsoft declined a Reuters request for comment. The Telegraph report said Nscale had faced repeated delays with the project. National power grid officials, it reported, had told Nscale they did not expect a power supply for the data center until the 2030s.

Nscale filed for an initial public offering in the US last month, with Microsoft and Anthropic expected to be its major customers, according to its prospectus. Nscale provides infrastructure, including compute, power and data centers, as well as software for training and running AI models.  The Nvidia-backed AI group, which competes against CoreWeave, Nebius, Crusoe and Lambda, has grown rapidly since its launch, scaling from $100 million to more than $103 billion in total contracted value in just two-and-a-half years.
